reigns.tagline: The vassal king who built the world's first superpower
reigns.previously: The Medes rule Iran from Ecbatana. Persis is a small vassal kingdom.
paragraphs: Around 550 BC the Medes ruled Iran from their capital, Ecbatana. Their king Astyages had a vassal in the south-west: Cyrus, king of Anshan in Persis. Herodotus says Cyrus was also his grandson. Cyrus rebelled, and when the Median army marched against him its general Harpagus switched sides. Ecbatana fell, and a minor Persian king suddenly owned an empire.

He kept going. He beat Croesus of Lydia, the richest king anyone knew of, and took his capital Sardis around 547 BC. In 539 BC Babylon opened its gates without a fight. Cyrus had a clay cylinder inscribed, boasting that he'd restored temples and let uprooted peoples go home. The exiled Jews went back to rebuild their Temple, and the Book of Isaiah calls him the Lord's anointed.

He built a garden capital at Pasargadae. Around 530 BC he marched against the Massagetae, horse nomads beyond the Caspian, and was killed. His plain stone tomb still stands at Pasargadae. His son Cambyses inherited an empire running from the Aegean to Central Asia.

claims.text: Astyages dreamed his baby grandson would replace him and ordered him killed. A herdsman raised Cyrus instead, and Harpagus, who had failed to kill the baby, was tricked into eating his own son.
claims.note: Herodotus tells it and admits he heard other versions. Abandoned babies who grow up to be kings are a classic folk-tale pattern.

claims.text: Queen Tomyris of the Massagetae dipped his severed head in a skin full of blood, so he could drink his fill.
claims.note: Herodotus calls it the most believable of the stories he heard. Xenophon has Cyrus die peacefully in bed, and Ctesias gives yet another death.

claims.text: The Cyrus Cylinder is the world's first charter of human rights.
claims.note: The cylinder is real and in the British Museum. Most historians read it as standard Babylonian royal propaganda; the human-rights label is a modern one.

reigns.hook: Cyrus's body comes home to Pasargadae. His eldest son Cambyses takes the throne, and he has his eye on the one great kingdom his father never touched: Egypt.

reigns.tagline: He conquered Egypt, and the Greeks called him mad
reigns.previously: Cyrus the Great is killed on the steppe, around 530 BC.
paragraphs: Cambyses took over the biggest empire on earth and set out to make it bigger. In 525 BC he beat the Egyptian army at Pelusium, on the edge of the Nile Delta, and took Memphis. The young pharaoh Psamtik III was captured. Cambyses was crowned pharaoh, took Egyptian titles, and Egypt's own records treat him as a proper king.

Greek writers remembered him very differently. Herodotus, writing a lifetime later and listening to Egyptian priests, paints a drunken madman who mocked the gods. He also tells of campaigns south into Nubia and west into the desert that went badly wrong.

Back home there was trouble. Before leaving for Egypt, Darius later claimed, Cambyses had secretly had his brother Bardiya killed. In 522 BC a man calling himself Bardiya seized the throne anyway. Cambyses turned for home to deal with him, but died on the way, in Syria, from a wound in his thigh.

claims.text: Cambyses stabbed the sacred Apis bull of Memphis in the thigh, and it died.
claims.note: Herodotus says so. But Egyptian inscriptions record an Apis bull buried with full honours in Cambyses's reign, which makes the story look like priestly spite.

claims.text: An army of 50,000 sent to the oasis of Siwa was swallowed by a sandstorm and never seen again.
claims.note: Only Herodotus tells it. Explorers have claimed to find traces in the desert, but nothing has been proved.

claims.text: His fatal wound came from his own sword, which slipped from its sheath as he leapt onto his horse.
claims.note: Herodotus again, who adds that it struck the same spot where he'd stabbed the Apis. Darius's Behistun inscription just says he died his own death.

reigns.hook: Cambyses is dead and has no son. On the throne sits a man who says he's Bardiya. Seven Persian nobles are sure he's a fake, and one of them is called Darius.

reigns.tagline: Seven conspirators, one horse, and a king of kings
reigns.cameToPower: Killed the king with six nobles
reigns.previously: Cambyses dies on the road home. A man called Bardiya holds the throne.
paragraphs: Darius told the story his way, carved on a cliff. The man on the throne wasn't Bardiya at all, he said, but a Magian priest named Gaumata in disguise. On 29 September 522 BC Darius and six fellow nobles cornered him in a fortress in Media and killed him. Then the empire exploded. Rebels rose in Babylon, Media, Persis and beyond, and Darius spent a year crushing them.

He had his version cut high on the rock at Behistun in three languages, Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian, above a relief of captive rebel kings roped together. He was a superb organiser: provinces called satrapies paying fixed tribute, a gold coin called the daric, and the Royal Road, with relay stations from Sardis to Susa.

He began the palace city of Persepolis. Around 513 BC he crossed into Europe against the Scythians, and in 499–494 BC he crushed a revolt of the Ionian Greeks. Athens had helped the rebels, and when the Athenians beat his punitive force at Marathon in 490 BC, he planned a bigger war. He died in late 486 BC, with Egypt in revolt, and was laid in a cliff tomb at Naqsh-e Rostam.

claims.text: The dead 'Bardiya' really was an impostor called Gaumata.
claims.note: That's Darius's own account at Behistun, echoed by Herodotus. Many historians suspect the real Bardiya was killed and the impostor story covered a coup.

claims.text: The seven agreed that whoever's horse neighed first at sunrise would be king, and Darius's groom rigged the contest.
claims.note: Herodotus tells it, with two versions of the groom's trick involving a mare. A good story written down long afterwards.

claims.text: The Behistun inscription was the key to reading cuneiform.
claims.note: Copied by Henry Rawlinson in the 1830s and 1840s, its Old Persian text let scholars crack Babylonian, much as the Rosetta Stone did for hieroglyphs.

reigns.hook: Darius leaves an unfinished war with Greece and a revolt in Egypt. His chosen heir is a younger son, Xerxes, whose mother Atossa is a daughter of Cyrus the Great.

reigns.tagline: He whipped the sea, burned Athens, and still lost
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Son of Darius I and Atossa
reigns.cameToPower: Chosen heir over an older half-brother
reigns.previously: Darius the Great dies in 486 BC, with Egypt in revolt.
paragraphs: Xerxes began by stamping out revolts in Egypt and Babylon. Then he turned to Greece. In 480 BC he crossed the Hellespont into Europe on bridges of boats lashed together, leading one of the largest armies the ancient world had seen. At Thermopylae a small Greek force under the Spartan king Leonidas held him up for days before being wiped out. Athens was emptied and burned.

Then it went wrong. In September 480 BC the Greek fleet lured his ships into the narrow strait of Salamis and smashed them, while Xerxes watched from a throne on the shore. He went home, leaving his general Mardonius behind. In 479 BC the Greeks beat Mardonius at Plataea, and the invasion was over. For the Greeks it became the founding story of their freedom.

At home he finished much of Persepolis, including the Gate of All Nations with its giant winged bulls. In 465 BC he was murdered in his palace in a plot led by Artabanus, a powerful official at court. In the bloody scramble that followed, a younger son, Artaxerxes, came out on top.

claims.text: When a storm wrecked his first bridge, Xerxes had the Hellespont given 300 lashes and the bridge builders beheaded.
claims.note: Herodotus tells it. Some historians think a Persian ritual was misunderstood or exaggerated by hostile Greeks.

claims.text: His army had 1.7 million infantry.
claims.note: That's Herodotus's figure. Modern estimates are far smaller, usually somewhere between about 100,000 and 300,000; feeding millions would have been impossible.

claims.text: He is King Ahasuerus of the Bible's Book of Esther.
claims.note: Ahasuerus is the Hebrew form of the name Xerxes, so most scholars make the link, but no Persian record backs up the Esther story.

reigns.hook: Xerxes is dead, and his eldest son Darius is soon killed too, blamed for the murder. The winner is a younger son, Artaxerxes, and he'll hold the throne for forty years.

reigns.title: Artaxerxes I and Darius II
reigns.tagline: Long hands, short reigns, and Persian gold for Sparta
reigns.previously: Xerxes is murdered in his palace in 465 BC.
paragraphs: Artaxerxes I ruled for about 40 years, and the Greeks nicknamed him Longimanus, the long-handed. Persia had lost the Aegean, but its kings had other weapons, mainly gold. Themistocles, the Athenian who won Salamis, was driven out of Athens and fled to Artaxerxes, who gave him cities to live off. The Bible says this king sent Ezra and then Nehemiah to Jerusalem to rebuild it.

When Artaxerxes died in 424 BC, the palace turned into a knife fight. His son Xerxes II lasted about 45 days before his half-brother Sogdianus had him killed. Another half-brother, Ochus, raised an army, overthrew Sogdianus and took the throne as Darius II.

Darius II leaned on his formidable wife and half-sister, Parysatis. When Athens and Sparta tore each other apart in the Peloponnesian War, Persian money paid for Sparta's fleet. Darius sent his and Parysatis's favourite son, the young Cyrus, west to Sardis to manage the war. Athens lost in 404 BC, and the same year Darius died.

claims.text: Artaxerxes I got his nickname because his right hand was longer than his left.
claims.note: Plutarch says so. 'Long-handed' may simply have meant a king with a long reach.

claims.text: Athens and Persia made a formal peace, the Peace of Callias, around 449 BC.
claims.note: Later Greek orators cite it, but Thucydides never mentions it, and the historian Theopompus called the text a forgery.

claims.text: Xerxes II reigned 45 days and Sogdianus about six and a half months.
claims.note: The figures come from Ctesias, a Greek doctor at the Persian court, who is colourful and often unreliable.

reigns.hook: Darius II's elder son becomes Artaxerxes II. But Queen Parysatis loves the younger one, Cyrus, best, and Cyrus has Spartan friends and plenty of Greek soldiers for hire.

reigns.title: Brothers, Mercenaries and Poison
reigns.tagline: A brother's revolt, a long march, and a poisoned knife
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Darius II's son and his heirs
reigns.previously: Darius II dies in 404 BC, as Athens loses its war with Sparta.
paragraphs: Artaxerxes II reigned longer than any other Achaemenid, from 404 to 358 BC, but it started badly. His younger brother Cyrus hired over 10,000 Greek mercenaries and marched on Babylon. At Cunaxa in 401 BC the Greeks won their part of the field, but Cyrus charged at his brother and was killed. The Greeks were stranded deep inside the empire, and their generals were lured to a parley and seized.

The Athenian Xenophon helped lead the rest out, north through the snowy mountains to the Black Sea, and wrote it all up as the Anabasis. Persia lost Egypt around 404 BC, but in the King's Peace of 387/386 BC the Greeks accepted Persian rule over the cities of Asia Minor. The Great King had become the referee of Greek politics.

His son Artaxerxes III (358–338 BC) was ruthless and effective, and won Egypt back around 343 BC. Then the eunuch Bagoas, his chief minister, poisoned him, put his son Arses on the throne as Artaxerxes IV, and poisoned him too in 336 BC. Across the sea, Philip II of Macedon was getting ready to invade.

claims.text: When the Ten Thousand finally saw the Black Sea, they shouted "The sea! The sea!"
claims.note: Xenophon was there and tells it himself, but his is the only account, written years later.

claims.text: Queen Parysatis poisoned her daughter-in-law Stateira with a knife greased on one side, carving a bird and eating the clean half herself.
claims.note: Plutarch, drawing on Ctesias, the court doctor. A great story from a writer with a taste for melodrama.

claims.text: Artaxerxes III killed most of his own relatives when he took the throne.
claims.note: Reported by later Greek and Roman writers such as Justin; the numbers and details can't be checked.

reigns.hook: Bagoas needs a new puppet and picks a royal cousin who seems safe. He isn't. And in Macedon, Philip's 20-year-old son Alexander has just become king.

reigns.tagline: The last Great King, chased across his own empire
reigns.cameToPower: Put on the throne by a poisoner
reigns.previously: The eunuch Bagoas poisons two kings in a row, the second in 336 BC.
paragraphs: Bagoas chose Darius III, a royal cousin, as a safe puppet. He wasn't. When Bagoas tried to poison him too, Darius made him drink the cup himself. But in 334 BC Alexander of Macedon crossed into Asia and beat the local Persian governors at the river Granicus.

Darius led the royal army himself at Issus in November 333 BC, and fled when the Macedonians broke through. He left behind his mother Sisygambis, his wife and his daughters. He offered land and a daughter's hand for peace, and Alexander said no. On 1 October 331 BC, at Gaugamela in northern Iraq, Darius fled again, and his empire went with him.

Babylon and Susa opened their gates. Darius fell back east to raise another army, but his own nobles had had enough. In July 330 BC Bessus, the satrap of Bactria, and his allies put the king in chains, stabbed him and left him dying in a wagon as Alexander's cavalry closed in.

claims.text: Darius forced Bagoas to drink the poison meant for him.
claims.note: Diodorus tells it, writing three centuries later. Neat, but Bagoas does disappear early in the reign.

claims.text: Alexander treated Darius's captive mother, wife and daughters with great honour.
claims.note: Arrian, Plutarch and others agree, but they were Alexander's admirers, writing centuries later.

claims.text: Alexander found Darius's body and covered it with his own cloak.
claims.note: Plutarch tells it. Other versions have Darius still alive, giving his last words to a Macedonian soldier.

reigns.hook: Darius gets a royal burial. Alexander now poses as his avenger and heir, while in Bactria the killer Bessus calls himself king. Iran has two would-be Great Kings, and one of them is Greek-speaking and 26.

reigns.tagline: He burned Persepolis, then dressed as a Persian king
reigns.previously: Darius III is stabbed by his own satrap and left to die in a wagon.
paragraphs: Alexander had been king of Macedon since he was 20. By spring 330 BC he held Persepolis, and before moving on he burned its palaces. After Darius died he hunted down Bessus, who had claimed the crown, and had him mutilated and executed. Then came years of hard fighting in Bactria and Sogdia, where in 327 BC he married Roxana, the daughter of a local noble.

To his Macedonians' disgust he started wearing Persian dress and asked Greeks to bow down to him in the Persian way, proskynesis. He pushed on into India, then led his army back through the Gedrosian desert, where thousands died. At Susa in 324 BC he held a mass wedding, taking Darius's daughter Stateira as a wife while his officers married Persian noblewomen.

In June 323 BC, in Babylon, he fell ill after a drinking party and died at 32. Iranians remembered him in two ways. Zoroastrian books call him 'the accursed Alexander', who burned the holy scriptures. Yet the Shahnameh makes him half Persian, a son of the Persian king Darab, so his conquest becomes a family affair.

claims.text: Persepolis was burned on a drunken whim, urged on by the Athenian courtesan Thaïs.
claims.note: Plutarch and Diodorus tell it. Arrian presents the burning as deliberate revenge for Xerxes burning Athens.

claims.text: Alexander was poisoned.
claims.note: Rumours spread fast, aimed at the family of his general Antipater. Most historians suspect illness, made worse by drink and old wounds. Even the day, 10 or 11 June, is disputed.

claims.text: Alexander was the son of the Persian king Darab and a Greek princess.
claims.note: Ferdowsi's Shahnameh, finished around 1010, borrowing from the Alexander Romance. It turns a foreign conqueror into a rightful Iranian heir.

reigns.hook: Alexander leaves no grown heir. His generals carve up the empire around two puppets, his half-brother Philip III and his baby son Alexander IV. Both will be murdered, and Iran goes to the toughest general left.

reigns.title: The Seleucid Kings
reigns.tagline: Greek kings, Indian elephants and a long slow retreat
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Alexander's former officer and his heirs
reigns.previously: Alexander's generals spend 11 years fighting over his empire.
paragraphs: When Alexander died, his officers went to war over the pieces. Seleucus, a Macedonian who had commanded the royal guard, won back Babylon in 312 BC. His followers counted their years from that moment and simply kept counting. The Seleucid Era was the first calendar of its kind, and people in the Near East used it for centuries. He swapped his Indian lands with Chandragupta Maurya for 500 war elephants, then used them to win at Ipsus in 301 BC.

Seleucus founded Seleucia on the Tigris and Antioch in Syria, and Greek-speaking settlers spread across Iran. In 281 BC he was struck down by Ptolemy Keraunos, a runaway Egyptian prince he had taken in. His heirs could not hold the far east. Around 250 BC their governor Diodotus made Bactria a kingdom of his own, and Parthia slipped away too.

Antiochus III, called the Great, marched east in 209 BC and made the Parthian king bow. Then he took on Rome and lost at Magnesia in 190 BC. Saddled with a vast war debt, he raided a temple in Elymais in 187 BC and the locals killed him. His son Antiochus IV died in Iran in 164 BC. Bit by bit the Parthians took Media, then Seleucia itself in 141 BC. The Seleucids were left with Syria.

claims.text: Seleucus traded his Indian provinces to Chandragupta Maurya for 500 war elephants.
claims.note: Strabo gives the figure, writing nearly three centuries later. A treaty and an elephant deal are widely accepted; the exact number is not.

claims.text: Antiochus III was killed by locals while plundering a temple of Bel in Elymais.
claims.note: Diodorus, Strabo and Justin all report it, though their details differ.

claims.text: The Seleucid Era, counted from 312 BC, stayed in use long after the Seleucids were gone.
claims.note: Syriac Christians and Jewish communities dated documents by it well into the Middle Ages.

reigns.hook: While the Seleucids look west, a band of steppe horsemen rides into their north-eastern province. Their leader is called Arsaces, and every king after him will use his name.

reigns.title: Arsaces and the Rise of Parthia
reigns.tagline: Steppe riders who named every king after their founder
reigns.previously: Seleucid Greeks rule Iran, but the far east is slipping away.
paragraphs: The Parni were nomads from the steppe east of the Caspian Sea, horsemen who lived by herding and raiding. Around 238 BC their chief Arsaces rode into Parthia, a Seleucid province in what is now north-eastern Iran and Turkmenistan, and killed its governor Andragoras. The newcomers took the province's name, and history has called them Parthians ever since. Their kings counted their years from 247 BC.

Arsaces started a habit that drives historians mad. Every king after him used the name Arsaces on his coins, so telling them apart is hard work. The coins show an archer sitting on a stool, in the soft cap of a steppe horseman. The early royal centres were Nisa, near modern Ashgabat, and Hecatompylos, the city of a hundred gates. When Antiochus III marched east in 209 BC, Arsaces II gave in and became his ally.

Once Antiochus went home, the Parthians grew again. Phriapatius and then Phraates I pushed west towards the Caspian shore. Still, this was a small frontier kingdom. The Seleucids held Media, Persis and Babylonia, the rich heart of the region. That was about to change.

claims.text: Arsaces killed the Seleucid governor Andragoras to take Parthia.
claims.note: Justin says so. Other writers tell it differently, Andragoras struck his own coins as if he had already broken away, and the dates vary by a decade.

claims.text: The dynasty began when two brothers, Arsaces and Tiridates, killed a Seleucid official who had made advances on Tiridates.
claims.note: From Arrian's lost history of Parthia, known only from a later summary. Tiridates may never have existed.

claims.text: Every Parthian king called himself Arsaces on his coins.
claims.note: The coins show it. Modern numbering of the kings is pieced together from other evidence and still changes.

reigns.hook: Then a new king, Mithridates, takes the throne with much bigger plans. Within a few decades the little steppe kingdom will be sitting in the Seleucids' greatest eastern city.

reigns.tagline: The king who turned a border state into an empire
reigns.cameToPower: Chosen by his brother Phraates I
reigns.previously: The Parthians have a small kingdom; the Seleucids hold the rich west.
paragraphs: Mithridates took over a frontier kingdom and left an empire. His brother Phraates had passed over his own sons to give him the crown, and he made it count. He fought the Greek kings of Bactria in the east, then turned west while the Seleucids were tearing themselves apart. Around 148 BC he took Media. In 141 BC he marched into Babylonia and took Seleucia on the Tigris, the great Greek city of the east.

He was a nomad's heir ruling Greeks and Babylonians, and he played it well. His coins called him Philhellene, friend of the Greeks, and he took up the old title Great King. When the Seleucid king Demetrius II came east to win it all back, the Parthians captured him in 138 BC. Mithridates treated him like an honoured guest, kept him in Hyrcania and gave him his daughter Rhodogune as a wife.
Mithridates died around 132 BC. His empire ran from Mesopotamia to the borders of Bactria, and his family would keep most of it for more than three and a half centuries.

claims.text: Mithridates married his daughter Rhodogune to his royal prisoner, Demetrius II.
claims.note: Appian and Justin both report it. Demetrius still tried to escape and was dragged back.

claims.text: He came to the throne around 171 BC.
claims.note: That is the traditional date. Some scholars argue for about 165 BC from the coins.

claims.text: He called himself Philhellene, friend of the Greeks.
claims.note: The word appears on his coins, aimed at the Greek cities he now ruled.

reigns.hook: His son Phraates II kills the Seleucid Antiochus VII in battle in 129 BC, then is killed by his own nomad mercenaries. His uncle Artabanus dies fighting nomads too. Parthia needs a saviour.

reigns.tagline: The first Parthian to call himself King of Kings
reigns.previously: Two Parthian kings in a row die fighting nomads from the steppe.
paragraphs: Mithridates II inherited a crisis. Nomads from Central Asia, the Saka among them, were pouring into the eastern provinces and had already killed two kings. He beat them back and won the east again. The Saka ended up in the south-east, in the land later named Sistan after them. He took Armenia's prince Tigranes as a hostage, then sent him home as a friendly king. On his coins he was the first Parthian to call himself King of Kings.

This was the age of the Silk Road. Envoys from Han China reached Parthia, which the Chinese called Anxi, and silk began to move west through Parthian hands. Then came the first meeting with Rome. Around 96 BC the king's envoy Orobazus met the Roman general Sulla on the Euphrates. Sulla set out three chairs and took the middle one, as if Rome were in charge. Back home, Orobazus paid for that with his life.

claims.text: The king had his envoy Orobazus executed for letting Sulla take the seat of honour.
claims.note: Plutarch is the only source, writing nearly two centuries later. The meeting is accepted; the execution can't be checked.

claims.text: The king of Anxi sent 20,000 horsemen to meet the first Han envoys at his eastern border.
claims.note: So says Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian. Which king it was, and the exact date, are argued over.

claims.text: He was the first Parthian king to use the title King of Kings.
claims.note: His coins carry it, an old Achaemenid title brought back to life.

reigns.hook: After him Parthia sinks into decades of rival kings, so murky that coin experts call it a dark age. It ends with a family crime: King Phraates III murdered by his own sons, Orodes and Mithridates.

reigns.tagline: Rome's richest man came east for glory and lost his head
reigns.cameToPower: Killed his father, then his brother
reigns.reignEnded: Murdered by his son Phraates IV
reigns.previously: Parthia's rival kings end with Phraates III murdered by his sons.
paragraphs: Orodes and his brother Mithridates killed their father together, then turned on each other. Mithridates fled to the Romans, came back with an army, was trapped in Babylon and executed in front of Orodes. Now Orodes had all of Parthia, and a Roman problem. Marcus Crassus, the richest man in Rome, wanted a war to match the glory of his partners Pompey and Caesar. In 53 BC he crossed the Euphrates.

At Carrhae, on the dry plains of northern Mesopotamia, the Parthian general Surena was waiting with horse archers and armoured lancers. Camels brought up fresh arrows so the archers never ran short. The legions could not catch them or get away. Crassus's son died in a charge, Crassus was killed at a parley, and around 20,000 Romans died. Rome's eagle standards went to Parthia as trophies.

Surena had done too well. Orodes, jealous, had him put to death. The king's son Pacorus raided deep into Roman Syria, but in 38 BC he was killed in battle. The grieving king made another son, Phraates, his heir. Phraates thanked him with murder.

claims.text: Crassus's severed head was used as a prop in a performance of Euripides's Bacchae at the Armenian court.
claims.note: Plutarch tells it in vivid detail, about 150 years later. No other source confirms it.

claims.text: The Parthians poured molten gold down Crassus's throat to mock his greed.
claims.note: Only Cassius Dio has it, around 250 years after the battle, and he hedges it with 'some say'.

claims.text: Phraates gave his sick father poison, and when it cured him instead, strangled him.
claims.note: Plutarch's neat twist makes historians wary. That Phraates killed Orodes is widely accepted.

reigns.hook: Phraates IV has the throne. Next he kills his brothers. And Mark Antony is gathering an army to avenge Crassus.

reigns.title: Phraates IV, Queen Musa and Rival Kings
reigns.tagline: A slave girl from Italy becomes queen of Parthia
reigns.previously: Orodes II, grieving for his son Pacorus, is murdered by Phraates.
paragraphs: Phraates IV began by killing his brothers. In 36 BC Mark Antony invaded with a huge army, besieged the Median royal city of Phraaspa and failed. His retreat through the mountains to Armenia, starving and harried by horse archers, cost him tens of thousands of men. In 20 BC Phraates made a deal with Augustus and handed back the standards lost by Crassus. Augustus hailed it as a triumph, and had it shown on the breastplate of his Prima Porta statue.

Augustus had also sent Phraates a gift: an Italian slave girl called Musa. She became his favourite, then his queen. She talked him into sending his four older sons to Rome as hostages, which cleared the way for her own boy. Around 2 BC Phraates died, poisoned by Musa, says the historian Josephus. She ruled beside her son, now Phraates V, and her portrait appears on the coins.

The nobles threw them out within a few years. Next they tried Vonones, a son raised in Rome, and mocked his Roman manners. Artabanus II, who had grown up among the Dahae nomads, won the throne and spent decades fighting rivals, and Rome, over Armenia. More pretenders and short reigns followed him.

claims.text: Musa poisoned Phraates IV to put her son on the throne.
claims.note: Josephus says so, about a century later. Nobody else describes how Phraates died.

claims.text: Musa married her own son, Phraates V.
claims.note: Josephus again, and the nobles' outrage is his explanation for their fall. It may be gossip.

claims.text: The return of Crassus's standards is shown on the breastplate of the Prima Porta statue of Augustus.
claims.note: The statue, found in 1863 and now in the Vatican, shows a Parthian handing over a standard.

reigns.hook: Around AD 51 a new king, Vologases I, takes the throne. He wants Armenia for his brother Tiridates, and Rome isn't going to like it.

reigns.title: Rome at the Gates
reigns.tagline: Rome sacks their capital three times. A Persian ends them
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Vologases I, son of Vonones II
reigns.previously: Rival Parthian kings fight each other, and Rome, for decades.
paragraphs: Vologases I wanted Armenia for his brother Tiridates, and Rome would not allow it. After years of war, a Roman army surrendered to the Parthians at Rhandeia in AD 62. The deal that followed was neat. A Parthian prince would rule Armenia, but he would get his crown from Rome. In 66 Tiridates travelled to Rome and bowed before Nero, who crowned him in a lavish show.

Later emperors came in force. Trajan took Ctesiphon, the Parthian capital, in 116 and reached the Persian Gulf, then pulled back. In 165 the army of Lucius Verus sacked Ctesiphon and Seleucia, and may have carried a terrible plague home. Septimius Severus sacked Ctesiphon again in 198. Caracalla asked for a Parthian princess, then fell on the wedding party, Herodian says.

Parthia hit back. In 217 Artabanus IV beat the emperor Macrinus at Nisibis, and Rome paid to end the war. The real danger was closer to home. In Persis, a local lord called Ardashir was building a kingdom. Around 28 April 224, at Hormozdgan, Ardashir defeated and killed Artabanus. The Arsacids had ruled for more than four centuries.

claims.text: Caracalla asked to marry a Parthian princess, then massacred the guests who came to meet him.
claims.note: Herodian tells it. Cassius Dio, who lived through it, says Caracalla attacked after the Parthian king turned down the marriage.

claims.text: Lucius Verus's soldiers brought the Antonine Plague back from Seleucia.
claims.note: Roman writers linked the plague to the sack. It may already have been spreading; the disease itself is uncertain.

claims.text: Nero crowned the Parthian prince Tiridates king of Armenia in Rome in AD 66.
claims.note: Suetonius and Cassius Dio both describe the ceremony.

reigns.hook: Ardashir rides away from Hormozdgan as master of Iran. Now he must show everyone that a new family, the Sasanians, rules by the will of the gods.

reigns.tagline: A lord from Persis topples Parthia and founds a dynasty
reigns.previously: Rome batters Parthia, then a lord from Persis kills its last king.
paragraphs: Ardashir came from Istakhr in Persis, the old Persian heartland near the ruins of Persepolis. His grandfather Sasan, the story goes, served at the temple of the goddess Anahita there, and his father Papak made himself a local king. Ardashir conquered his neighbours one by one, then took on the Parthian king Artabanus IV. At Hormozdgan in 224 he killed him and became King of Kings of the Iranians.

He made sure everyone got the message. At Naqsh-e Rostam, below the tombs of the old Achaemenid kings, he had himself carved on horseback taking the ring of kingship from the god Ahura Mazda. Under his horse lies Artabanus. Under the god's horse lies Ahriman, the spirit of evil. Ardashir backed a Zoroastrian state church, and later tradition says the priest Tansar helped him build it.

Then he turned on Rome. He pushed into Roman Mesopotamia, and around 240 he took Hatra, the desert city that had beaten off two Roman emperors. By then he had made his son Shapur co-ruler. Around 242 Ardashir died, and Shapur had the throne to himself.

claims.text: Ardashir escaped the Parthian court with the king's slave girl, and a great ram, the spirit of royal glory, ran after him.
claims.note: From the Kar-namag i Ardashir, a Middle Persian romance written down centuries later. It reads like a folk tale.

claims.text: Sasan was Ardashir's grandfather.
claims.note: Shapur's inscription and al-Tabari say so. The Kar-namag makes Sasan his real father, with Papak as his mother's father.

claims.text: The priest Tansar wrote a letter defending Ardashir's new order.
claims.note: The letter survives only in a 13th-century Persian version of a lost Arabic translation. How much is Ardashir's era is argued over.

reigns.hook: Shapur inherits his father's war with Rome. Over the next twenty years three Roman emperors will face him: one dies, one pays, and one becomes his prisoner.

reigns.tagline: The King of Kings who took a Roman emperor prisoner
reigns.previously: Ardashir I topples the Parthians and makes his son Shapur co-ruler.
paragraphs: Shapur fought Rome three times and won three times, and he made sure nobody forgot. In 244 the young emperor Gordian III died after a battle at Misiche on the Euphrates. His successor, Philip the Arab, bought peace for 500,000 denarii. In 253 Shapur smashed a Roman army at Barbalissos and went on to sack Antioch, the great city of Roman Syria.

Then came the big one. In 260, near Edessa, the emperor Valerian was captured along with his officers. No Roman emperor had ever been taken by a foreign enemy before. Shapur had his triumphs carved into the cliffs at Naqsh-e Rostam and Bishapur, with Roman emperors at his horse's feet. On the Ka'ba-ye Zartosht he put up his own account of it all in Middle Persian, Parthian and Greek.

Thousands of Roman prisoners were settled in Iran, where they built new towns and, so it's said, the Band-e Kaisar dam at Shushtar. Shapur also welcomed the prophet Mani, whose new faith blended ideas from Zoroaster, the Buddha and Jesus. His last years were less glorious. Odaenathus of Palmyra, fighting on Rome's side, raided deep into Persian Mesopotamia. Shapur died around 270.

claims.text: Shapur used the captive Valerian as a mounting block, and had his skin stuffed and hung in a temple after he died.
claims.note: Told by Lactantius, a Christian writer who saw Valerian's fate as God punishing a persecutor. No Persian source mentions it.

claims.text: Gordian III was killed in battle against Shapur.
claims.note: Shapur's inscription says so. Roman writers say he died later, perhaps murdered by his own officers.

claims.text: Valerian's captured soldiers built the Band-e Kaisar, the 'Caesar's dam', at Shushtar.
claims.note: Later Persian and Arab tradition says so and the name fits, but nothing written at the time confirms it.

reigns.hook: Shapur's sons take turns on the throne. And the high priest Kartir has decided that Mani, the prophet Shapur protected, is a dangerous heretic.

reigns.title: Mani, Kartir and Narseh
reigns.tagline: A prophet dies in chains and a priest takes charge
reigns.relationToPredecessor: Sons and grandsons of Shapur I
reigns.previously: Shapur I, the king who caught a Roman emperor, dies about 270.
paragraphs: Shapur's sons didn't have his luck. Hormizd I lasted about a year. Bahram I came next and turned on Mani, the prophet his father had welcomed. Mani taught that the world was a battle between light and darkness, and he wanted his faith to take in all the others. Bahram had him chained up, and Mani died in prison some time in the mid 270s. His religion spread from Roman Africa to China anyway.

Behind the throne stood Kartir, the high priest. He had his own boasts carved into the rocks beside the kings', listing the Jews, Christians, Buddhists, Manichaeans and others he had hounded. Bahram II ruled for nearly twenty years with Kartir at his side. His son Bahram III got the crown in 293 and lost it within months to his great-uncle Narseh, who told his side of the story on a huge inscription at Paikuli.

Then Narseh went after Rome. He beat the Roman Caesar Galerius once, but in 298 Galerius caught him off guard, routed him and captured his wives and children. At Nisibis in 299 Narseh gave up lands beyond the Tigris to make peace. His son Hormizd II died in 309, and the nobles took no chances with Hormizd's grown sons. They were killed, blinded or locked away.

claims.text: Kartir boasted of striking at Jews, Christians, Buddhists, Manichaeans and other faiths.
claims.note: His own inscriptions, including one on the Ka'ba-ye Zartosht, say so. How far he really went is harder to tell.

claims.text: Mani was flayed and his stuffed skin hung over a city gate.
claims.note: Later Muslim-era writers tell this. Manichaean texts say he died in chains after weeks in prison.

claims.text: The nobles killed or blinded Hormizd II's grown sons to clear the way for a baby.
claims.note: Told by al-Tabari and other later writers. One son, also called Hormizd, later escaped to the Romans.

reigns.hook: The grown princes are out of the way, and the nobles need a king. They choose one who hasn't been born yet.

reigns.tagline: Crowned in the womb, king for seventy years
reigns.cameToPower: Nobles crowned him as a baby
reigns.previously: Hormizd II is dead and the nobles have purged his grown sons.
paragraphs: The story goes that the nobles laid the crown on his pregnant mother's belly. True or not, Shapur II was a baby when he became king, and the great families ran Iran for him. They did a poor job. Arab raiders crossed the Gulf and plundered the coast. When Shapur grew up he hit back hard, raiding deep into Arabia, and Arab writers later gave him a grim nickname: the man of the shoulders.

Then Rome turned Christian, and Shapur began to see Persia's Christians as Rome's friends. From the 340s he squeezed them with double taxes and executions, and Syriac writers kept the memory of the martyrs. His wars with Rome dragged on for decades. In 359 he took the fortress of Amida after a long siege. A Roman officer, Ammianus Marcellinus, was inside, slipped out as it fell and wrote it all down.

In 363 the emperor Julian marched all the way to Ctesiphon, couldn't take it and turned back. He was killed in a skirmish on the retreat. His successor Jovian, stuck with a hungry army, handed back Nisibis and the lands Narseh had lost. Shapur also fought the Kushans and Huns in the east. When he died in 379, after about seventy years on the throne, Persia was stronger than it had been in generations.

claims.text: Shapur was crowned before he was born, the crown laid on his mother's belly.
claims.note: Agathias and al-Tabari tell it centuries later. He may simply have been a small baby when crowned.

claims.text: He pierced the shoulders of Arab captives and led them away on ropes, earning the name Dhu'l-Aktaf.
claims.note: This is al-Tabari's explanation. Other Arab writers explain the nickname differently.

claims.text: Ammianus Marcellinus was inside Amida in 359 and escaped when it fell.
claims.note: He tells the story himself, as an eyewitness, in Book 19 of his history.

reigns.hook: Shapur leaves a strong state behind. Keeping it is another matter. The next kings fall to murder, a phantom horse and the White Huns.

reigns.title: Bahram Gur and the White Huns
reigns.tagline: A hunter king, a phantom horse and a hidden trench
reigns.previously: Shapur II dies after about seventy years on the throne.
paragraphs: Three kings came and went in twenty years after Shapur, each ending in murder or deposition. Then came Yazdegerd I, who let Christians and Jews worship in peace. The priests hated him for it and called him the Sinner. Their revenge came in the story of his death: a beautiful horse rose out of a spring, kicked him dead and vanished back into the water.

His son Bahram V had been raised by the Arab kings of al-Hira, and later poets adored him. They called him Bahram Gur, after the wild ass he loved to hunt. He beat off nomads in the east and ruled from 420 to 438. Legend says he vanished while chasing game, swallowed by a swamp or a pit. His son Yazdegerd II crushed an Armenian Christian revolt at Avarayr in 451.

Peroz, king from 459, met a tougher enemy, the Hephthalites or White Huns. They captured him once and he had to be ransomed. At home a terrible famine struck. In 484 he went back to fight them, and he and much of his army died. Procopius says the Huns had dug a hidden trench and the Persian cavalry charged straight into it.

claims.text: Bahram V won his crown by taking it from between two lions.
claims.note: Told by al-Tabari and the Shahnameh. The nobles wanted another king, so Bahram proposed a test of courage.

claims.text: Yazdegerd I was killed by a horse that came out of a spring and vanished.
claims.note: Al-Tabari and the Shahnameh tell it. It reads like the priests' verdict on a king they hated.

claims.text: The emperor Arcadius asked Yazdegerd I to protect his little son Theodosius II.
claims.note: Procopius tells it over a century later. Earlier Roman writers don't mention it.

reigns.hook: Peroz is dead and the Huns want tribute. His brother Balash takes over, but one of Peroz's sons has spent years among the Huns.

reigns.tagline: The king who got out of jail in his wife's clothes
reigns.previously: Peroz falls to the White Huns. His brother Balash is deposed.
paragraphs: Kavad grew up as a hostage among the White Huns, and in 488, after his uncle Balash was thrown out and blinded, he took the throne with their help. The treasury was empty and the country was still reeling from famine. Kavad backed a radical preacher called Mazdak, who said the world's goods should be shared out. Poor people liked the idea. The great families and the priests did not.

In 496 they deposed him, gave the crown to his brother Jamasp and locked Kavad in the Castle of Oblivion, a prison so feared that, Procopius says, you weren't allowed to mention who was in it. His wife came to visit, swapped clothes with him, and he walked out. He fled to the Huns and came back with an army in 498 or 499. Jamasp stepped aside.

Kavad needed money to pay the Huns, so he went to war with Rome and took Amida in 503. Late in life he turned on the Mazdakites, and his son Khosrow led the slaughter. In 530 a young Roman general named Belisarius beat a Persian army at Dara. Kavad died in September 531, having picked Khosrow over his older sons.

claims.text: Kavad escaped prison by swapping clothes with his wife.
claims.note: Procopius tells it. Other sources say he escaped with help from friends.

claims.text: Mazdak preached that women, as well as property, should be shared.
claims.note: Only his enemies say so: Zoroastrian priests and later Muslim writers. No Mazdakite writings survive.

claims.text: Khosrow had the Mazdakites buried upside down, a garden of human trees.
claims.note: This grim scene comes from the Shahnameh, written about 500 years later.

reigns.tagline: The model just king, who also sacked Antioch
reigns.previously: Kavad I dies, passing over his older sons for Khosrow.
paragraphs: Later Persians and Arabs remembered Khosrow as the perfect just king, Anushirvan, of the immortal soul. He began by clearing out rival brothers. In 532 he made an Eternal Peace with Justinian, and the Romans paid a fortune in gold for it. Eight years later he broke it, sacked Antioch and marched its people home. He built them a new city near Ctesiphon and called it Khosrow's Better Antioch.

At home he rebuilt the state. Land was surveyed and taxed at fixed rates, and cavalrymen got pay and kit from the crown, so the king leaned less on the great lords. Greek philosophers pushed out of Athens came to his court hoping for a philosopher king. They went home disappointed. Chess arrived from India, and the story goes that his vizier Bozorgmehr answered it by inventing backgammon.

Around 560 he joined forces with the Turks and destroyed the White Huns, who had killed his grandfather. About 570 he sent a force to Yemen and drove out its Ethiopian rulers. The great brick arch at Ctesiphon, the Taq Kasra, still carries his name. He died about 579, and the crown passed to his son Hormizd IV.

claims.text: Khosrow's vizier Bozorgmehr invented backgammon to answer India's gift of chess.
claims.note: A Middle Persian text and the Shahnameh tell it. Bozorgmehr himself may be legendary.

claims.text: The Taq Kasra, the great arch at Ctesiphon, was built by Khosrow I.
claims.note: Tradition says so, but some scholars date it to Shapur I, three centuries earlier.

claims.text: The Greek philosophers found his court a letdown and went home.
claims.note: Agathias, a Greek writer with little love for Khosrow, is the source.

reigns.hook: Hormizd IV falls out with the nobles, then insults Bahram Chobin, the general who has just saved his empire. A general with an army doesn't take insults quietly.

reigns.tagline: He came close to beating Rome, then lost it all
reigns.reignEnded: Overthrown and killed by his son
reigns.previously: Hormizd IV has fallen out with his nobles and his best general.
paragraphs: In 590 a palace coup tied to Khosrow's uncles blinded his father and then killed him. Khosrow got the crown but couldn't keep it. The general Bahram Chobin marched on Ctesiphon and made himself king, and Khosrow ran to the Roman emperor Maurice. In 591 he came back with a Roman army, beat Bahram and took his throne back.

Khosrow loved luxury. He and his black horse Shabdiz are carved in the rock grotto at Taq-e Bostan. Poets made a love story of his Christian wife Shirin and Farhad, the sculptor who cut through a mountain for her. When the usurper Phocas murdered Maurice in 602, Khosrow invaded Roman lands as the dead emperor's avenger, and kept going for twenty years.

His armies took Antioch in 613 and Jerusalem in 614, carrying off the True Cross. Egypt fell in 619. In 626 a Persian army camped across the water from Constantinople while the Avars attacked it. Then the emperor Heraclius struck deep into Iran, won at Nineveh in December 627 and sacked Khosrow's palace at Dastagird. In February 628 Khosrow's son Kavad II overthrew him, and he was killed days later.

claims.text: The sculptor Farhad carved through a mountain for love of Shirin.
claims.note: Shirin was real. Farhad's story grows in later poems, above all Nizami's Khosrow and Shirin (12th century).

claims.text: Khosrow tore up a letter from the Prophet Muhammad inviting him to Islam.
claims.note: Islamic tradition tells it. No Persian or Roman source of the time mentions the letter.

claims.text: The Taq-e Bostan carvings show Khosrow II on his horse Shabdiz.
claims.note: The great grotto is usually dated to his reign. A few scholars have argued for another king.

reigns.hook: Kavad II makes peace with Heraclius and gets rid of his brothers. Within months he's dead too, and the crown starts changing hands at a dizzying rate.

reigns.title: The Collapse of the Sasanian Court
reigns.tagline: Four years, a blur of crowns and two queens
reigns.previously: Khosrow II is overthrown by his son Kavad II and killed.
paragraphs: Kavad II made peace with Heraclius and agreed to hand back what his father had taken. He also had his brothers killed, so no one could challenge him. Then plague swept the land, and within months it took him too. His little son Ardashir III was murdered in 630 by the general Shahrbaraz, who seized the throne, lasted about forty days and was killed in his turn.

Next came Boran, Khosrow's daughter and the first woman to rule Iran in her own right. She tried to calm things down and put her own face on the coins. Her sister Azarmidokht ruled briefly too. Around them buzzed a swarm of short-lived kings and claimants, so many that the sources can't agree on their order. The royal house had all but killed itself off.

In June 632 the nobles found a boy, Khosrow's grandson Yazdegerd, and crowned him at Istakhr. Zoroastrians still count their years from that day. A week earlier, far away in Medina, the Prophet Muhammad had died. The Arab tribes he had united were about to burst out of Arabia.

claims.text: Kavad II had seventeen or eighteen of his brothers killed.
claims.note: The numbers come from later sources and vary. That he wiped out his brothers is widely reported.

claims.text: Boran put her own portrait on her coins.
claims.note: Her silver coins survive in museum collections.

claims.text: The Zoroastrian calendar still counts from Yazdegerd III's coronation in 632.
claims.note: The Yazdegerdi era is still used by Zoroastrians in Iran and by the Parsis of India.

reigns.hook: The new king is a boy with a broken empire. Within a year, Arab armies are raiding Iraq.

reigns.tagline: The last King of Kings, running for his life
reigns.previously: Four years of chaos end with a boy king crowned at Istakhr.
paragraphs: Yazdegerd was a boy, and his generals ran the war. It came fast. The caliph Umar sent Arab armies into Iraq, and at al-Qadisiyyah, in 636 or 637, the Persian commander Rostam Farrokhzad was killed and the royal banner was captured. Ctesiphon fell soon after. The Arabs found a vast garden carpet woven with gold and jewels, the Spring of Khosrow, and cut it up to share out.

Yazdegerd fled up onto the Iranian plateau. A last big army gathered at Nahavand in 642, and the Arabs called their win there the victory of victories. After that Persia had no field army left. The king moved from city to city, always further east, with a shrinking court and a dwindling treasure.

In 651 he reached Merv, where the local governor turned against him. The best-known story says he hid in a mill and the miller killed him for his fine clothes. His son Peroz fled all the way to Tang China and asked the emperor for help. It never came. More than four centuries of Sasanian rule were over.

claims.text: Yazdegerd was killed by a miller who wanted his rich clothes.
claims.note: Al-Tabari gives this and other versions. Some blame the governor of Merv.

claims.text: The Arabs cut up the jewelled Spring of Khosrow carpet and shared out the pieces.
claims.note: Al-Tabari describes it. The size and splendour may have grown in the telling.

claims.text: Yazdegerd's son Peroz asked the Tang emperor for help.
claims.note: Chinese records note his embassies and his stay at the Tang court.

reigns.hook: Iran now belongs to the caliphs in Medina. Within ten years the caliphate itself splits, and a family based in Damascus takes it over.

reigns.title: Under the Caliphs
reigns.tagline: Iran gets new masters, and a new faith, slowly
reigns.reignEnded: Umayyads beaten on the Great Zab
reigns.previously: Yazdegerd III, last of the Sasanians, is murdered near Merv.
paragraphs: Iran was now a province of someone else's empire, ruled from Medina and then, from 661, by the Umayyad caliphs in Damascus. Zoroastrians kept their fire temples but paid the jizya, a tax on protected non-Muslims. Most Iranians stayed Zoroastrian for generations. Some left. One group sailed to Gujarat in India, and their descendants are the Parsis.

Converts found that Islam came with fine print. Persian Muslims, called mawali, were often treated as second class by their Arab masters. Around 700 the tax offices switched from Persian to Arabic. Far to the west, in 680, the Prophet's grandson Husayn was killed at Karbala, a death Shi'a Muslims still mourn every year. Iran would one day become the great Shi'a land, but not for eight centuries.

Anger boiled over in Khorasan, in the north-east. In 747 a shadowy organiser called Abu Muslim raised black banners there for the Abbasids, a family descended from the Prophet's uncle. Khorasani armies swept west, and in January 750 they smashed the last Umayyad caliph's army on the Great Zab river in Iraq.

claims.text: Zoroastrian refugees landed in Gujarat and were let in on conditions set by a local Hindu king.
claims.note: The tale comes from the Qissa-i Sanjan, written around 1600, long after the events.

claims.text: Most Iranians converted to Islam only in the 9th and 10th centuries.
claims.note: Richard Bulliet argued this from Muslim name lists. Other historians question his method.

claims.text: The tax offices in Iran switched from Persian to Arabic around 700.
claims.note: Arab historians tie the change to the governor al-Hajjaj. The year varies by province.

reigns.hook: The Abbasids have won with Persian swords. Now Abu Muslim, the man who won it for them, looks a little too powerful.

reigns.title: Persians at the Caliph's Court
reigns.tagline: The caliphs move east and start to rule like shahs
reigns.previously: The Umayyads are beaten on the Great Zab. The Abbasids take over.
paragraphs: The new caliphs owed everything to Khorasan, and they didn't trust it. In 755 the caliph al-Mansur summoned Abu Muslim and had him cut down. Then he built a new capital. Baghdad, founded in 762, rose on the Tigris not far from the ruins of Ctesiphon, and its court soon looked a lot like a Sasanian one, full of ceremony, viziers and Persian officials.

The greatest of those officials were the Barmakids, a family from Balkh whose ancestors had run a Buddhist monastery. They ran the empire for Harun al-Rashid, the caliph of the Thousand and One Nights. In 803 Harun turned on them overnight. The vizier Ja'far was beheaded and the rest were locked up. Nobody is quite sure why. Harun died at Tus in Khorasan in 809.

His sons fought over the throne. Al-Ma'mun, whose mother was Persian, ruled from Merv, and his general Tahir beat his brother's army and took Baghdad in 813. Al-Ma'mun named the Shi'a Imam Ali al-Rida his heir, but the Imam died suddenly at Tus in 818. His tomb grew into the holy city of Mashhad. In 821 Tahir became governor of Khorasan, and his family held on to it like a crown.

claims.text: Al-Mansur had Abu Muslim murdered in 755.
claims.note: All the main Arabic histories, al-Tabari's included, describe the killing.

claims.text: Harun destroyed the Barmakids because Ja'far secretly married Harun's sister Abbasa.
claims.note: One of several explanations in al-Tabari and later writers. Historians suspect plain fear of their power.

claims.text: Imam Ali al-Rida was poisoned on al-Ma'mun's orders.
claims.note: Shi'a tradition says so. Sunni sources say he died of illness, some say from eating grapes.

reigns.hook: Tahir's family rule Khorasan as kings in all but name. Others will soon go further, and Persian will become a language of poetry again.

reigns.title: Persian Revival
reigns.tagline: The caliph's grip slips, and Persian finds its voice again
reigns.previously: Tahir gets Khorasan, and his family keep it like a kingdom.
paragraphs: On paper the caliph in Baghdad still ruled Iran. In practice it was slipping away, province by province. Tahir's family ran Khorasan. In Sistan a tough upstart called Ya'qub ibn al-Layth, nicknamed the Coppersmith, carved out a kingdom with his sword and marched to within striking distance of Baghdad. Then the Samanids, ruling from Bukhara, built the brightest court in the east.

Under the Samanids something huge happened. Persian came back as a written language, now in Arabic letters, and poets like Rudaki wrote verse in it. In the west the Buyids, Shi'a soldiers from the mountains of Daylam, took Baghdad itself in 945 and kept the caliph as a figurehead. In the east the Turkish sultan Mahmud of Ghazni got rich raiding India.

It was an age of genius. Ferdowsi finished the Shahnameh, the giant epic of Iran's kings and heroes, around 1010. Avicenna wrote his Canon of Medicine, which doctors used for centuries. But on the steppe a new Turkish clan was on the move. In 1040 the Seljuks beat Mahmud's son Mas'ud at Dandanaqan, and Khorasan was theirs.

claims.text: Mahmud promised Ferdowsi gold for the Shahnameh, paid him in silver, and the insulted poet gave the money away.
claims.note: First told by Nizami Aruzi more than a century later, who says Ferdowsi split the silver between a bath attendant and a drinks seller.

claims.text: Ya'qub ibn al-Layth started out as a coppersmith.
claims.note: His nickname al-Saffar means coppersmith, and Arab historians say he worked the trade as a young man. Little else is known of his early life.

claims.text: The Samanid court made Persian a language of books again.
claims.note: Rudaki's surviving poems and the Persian version of al-Tabari's history made for a Samanid vizier, Bal'ami, are early proof.

reigns.hook: The Seljuks are nomads with tents and herds, but they think big. Next stop is Baghdad, where the caliph is looking for a new protector.

reigns.title: The Great Seljuks
reigns.tagline: Turkish sultans, a Persian vizier and the Assassins
reigns.previously: The Seljuk Turks beat the Ghaznavids at Dandanaqan.
paragraphs: The Seljuks were Turkish nomads, fresh converts to Sunni Islam, and they moved fast. In 1055 Tughril Beg rode into Baghdad, threw out the Buyids, and the grateful caliph named him sultan. His nephew Alp Arslan went further. In 1071 he smashed a Byzantine army at Manzikert and took the emperor Romanos IV prisoner, opening Anatolia to the Turks.

Alp Arslan's son Malik-Shah left the running of the empire to a brilliant Persian, the vizier Nizam al-Mulk. Nizam wrote a handbook for kings, the Book of Government, and founded colleges called Nizamiyyas. Omar Khayyam, famous today for his verses, helped build a new solar calendar in 1079. Iran's calendar today descends from it.

Then came the knives. In 1090 the Ismaili preacher Hasan-i Sabbah took the mountain castle of Alamut, and his followers, the Assassins, began killing their enemies. Nizam al-Mulk was stabbed in 1092 and Malik-Shah died weeks later. Heirs fought, and the empire split. Sultan Sanjar was captured by Oghuz nomads in 1153. In 1194 the last Seljuk sultan in Iran, Tughril III, fell in battle against the Khwarazmshah Tekish.

claims.text: The Assassins killed Nizam al-Mulk.
claims.note: His killer came disguised as a Sufi, and the Ismailis later took the credit. Some historians suspect the sultan or rivals at court were behind it.

claims.text: Nizam al-Mulk, Omar Khayyam and Hasan-i Sabbah were schoolfriends who swore to help each other rise.
claims.note: A later Persian tale made famous in English by Edward FitzGerald. Nizam was born about 30 years before the other two, so it can't be true.

claims.text: Omar Khayyam worked on Malik-Shah's calendar reform.
claims.note: Medieval writers name him among the astronomers the sultan gathered for the job.

reigns.hook: The Khwarazmshahs now rule most of Iran. Far to the east a Mongol chief named Temüjin has united the steppe tribes under a new title: Genghis Khan.

reigns.title: The Mongols and the Ilkhanate
reigns.tagline: Genghis Khan's storm, then Hulagu's khans in Tabriz
reigns.reignEnded: Abu Sa'id died without an heir
reigns.previously: The Seljuks are gone. The Khwarazmshahs rule Iran.
paragraphs: The Khwarazmshah Muhammad II ruled a big new empire, and he made a fatal mistake. In 1218 his governor at Otrar killed the merchants of a Mongol trade caravan, and when Genghis Khan sent envoys to complain they were killed or humiliated. In 1219 the Mongols came. Muhammad fled west and died on an island in the Caspian Sea.

The Mongols showed no mercy to cities that resisted. In 1221 Merv and Nishapur were destroyed and their people massacred. The chroniclers' death tolls run into the hundreds of thousands and beyond. Historians think those figures are inflated, but the killing was real, and Khorasan took generations to recover. In the 1250s Genghis's grandson Hulagu arrived, crushed the Assassins in 1256 and sacked Baghdad in 1258.

Hulagu's family, the Ilkhans, ruled Iran from Maragheh and later Tabriz. The scholar Nasir al-Din Tusi got a great observatory at Maragheh. In 1295 the Ilkhan Ghazan became a Muslim, and his vizier Rashid al-Din wrote a history of the whole known world before he was executed in 1318. Öljaitü built a vast domed tomb at Soltaniyeh. When Abu Sa'id died without an heir in 1335, the Ilkhanate fell apart.

claims.text: The last Abbasid caliph was rolled in a carpet and trampled to death by horses.
claims.note: Several sources say so, explaining it by a Mongol taboo against spilling royal blood. Other accounts give him different deaths.

claims.text: Hundreds of thousands, even more than a million, died at Merv and Nishapur.
claims.note: The figures come from chroniclers such as Ibn al-Athir and Juzjani. Modern historians think the real numbers were far lower, though still terrible.

claims.text: Rashid al-Din wrote a history of the whole known world.
claims.note: His Compendium of Chronicles covers the Mongols, China, India, the Franks and more. Copies made in Tabriz in his lifetime survive.

reigns.hook: With the Ilkhans gone, Iran breaks into little kingdoms. In Shiraz a poet named Hafez writes about wine and love. In Central Asia a lame warlord is building an army.

reigns.title: Timur and the Turkmen
reigns.tagline: Towers of skulls, a poet's mole and the Sheep tribes
reigns.previously: Abu Sa'id dies without an heir, and the Ilkhanate falls apart.
paragraphs: After the Ilkhans, Iran was a patchwork. The Jalayirids held Baghdad and Tabriz, the Muzaffarids held Shiraz, and smaller lords fought over the rest. Shiraz had Hafez, whose love poems are still quoted in Iranian homes today. Then, from 1381, Timur invaded. He was a Turk from near Samarkand, lame in one leg, and Europeans called him Tamerlane.

Timur was a military genius and a terror. When Isfahan rebelled in 1387, his soldiers killed a huge part of its population and piled the heads into towers. After he died in 1405 his son Shah Rukh ruled from Herat in a gentler style. Shah Rukh's wife Gawhar Shad built the great mosque at Mashhad, and their son Ulugh Beg built an observatory at Samarkand.

In the west two Turkmen tribal confederations, the Black Sheep and the White Sheep, fought over the Iranian plateau. The White Sheep chief Uzun Hasan won, then lost to the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II at Otlukbeli in 1473. Uzun Hasan's daughter married Haydar, head of a Sufi order at Ardabil, the Safavids. Their son would change Iran forever.

claims.text: Timur built towers of 70,000 skulls at Isfahan.
claims.note: The number comes from Timur's own court historians, who liked big figures. Nobody counted.

claims.text: Timur scolded Hafez for offering to give away Samarkand and Bukhara for a beauty's mole, and Hafez joked that such generosity was why he was poor.
claims.note: A much-loved tale that first appears long after both men were dead.

claims.text: Gawhar Shad built the great mosque at Mashhad in 1418.
claims.note: The mosque's dated inscription, written out by her son Baysunghur, names her as its founder.

reigns.hook: In 1501 a boy of about 14 rides into Tabriz at the head of red-capped warriors who think he is more than human. His name is Ismail.

reigns.tagline: The boy saint-king who made Iran Shi'a
reigns.previously: Uzun Hasan's grandson is about to ride out of hiding.
paragraphs: Ismail's father and eldest brother, leaders of the Safavid Sufi order, were both killed in battle, and the small boy was hidden away in Gilan by the Caspian. His followers were Turkmen tribesmen called the Qizilbash, the red heads, for their red caps with twelve folds, one for each Shi'a Imam. They saw him as more than human. In 1501 they beat the White Sheep and crowned him at Tabriz.

Then Ismail did something enormous. He made Twelver Shi'ism the religion of the state and forced it on his subjects, violently where they resisted. Most Iranians were Sunni then; within a few generations most were Shi'a, and they still are. In 1510 he beat the Uzbek khan Muhammad Shaybani near Merv. He also wrote poems in Azeri Turkish under the pen name Khata'i.

His aura of invincibility died at Chaldiran on 23 August 1514. The Ottoman sultan Selim I had cannon and Janissaries with guns, and the Qizilbash horsemen were cut to pieces. Tabriz was briefly occupied. Ismail never led an army into battle again. He died in 1524, aged 36, and left the throne to a ten-year-old son.

claims.text: Ismail turned Shaybani Khan's skull into a gold-covered drinking cup.
claims.note: Chroniclers writing at the time report it, and trophy skulls were not unknown on the steppe. No cup survives.

claims.text: His followers believed he was divine.
claims.note: His own poems as Khata'i present him as a holy figure close to God, and visitors to Iran reported the devotion of the Qizilbash.

claims.text: After Chaldiran he gave up on government and took to drink.
claims.note: Safavid chroniclers describe him hunting and drinking in his last years. Some historians think the story of a broken man is overdone.

reigns.hook: The new shah, Tahmasp, is ten years old. The Qizilbash chiefs who are supposed to guard him are already reaching for their swords.

reigns.tagline: Fifty-two years on a throne he got at ten
reigns.previously: Ismail I dies at 36. His heir is a boy of ten.
paragraphs: For his first ten years Tahmasp was a pawn. Qizilbash chiefs fought each other for control of the boy, and the country slid into civil war. The Ottoman sultan Suleiman the Magnificent invaded again and again, and Tabriz changed hands. Tahmasp learned to survive by playing the chiefs off against each other, and he moved his capital away from the border to Qazvin.

In 1544 an unexpected guest arrived: Humayun, the Mughal emperor, driven out of India. Tahmasp sheltered him and lent him troops to win his throne back. In 1555 the Peace of Amasya, the first formal peace with the Ottomans, settled the border for a generation. As a young man Tahmasp loved painting, and his workshop made one of the most lavish Shahnamehs ever, with 258 paintings.

Then he turned pious. He gave up wine, lost interest in art and closed the taverns. In 1562 he handed the runaway Ottoman prince Bayezid and his sons over to Ottoman executioners, in return for gold. He reigned 52 years, longer than any other Safavid. When he died in 1576 he had not settled the succession, and his sons went for each other's throats.

claims.text: Tahmasp was poisoned.
claims.note: Rumours of poison went round the court, as they often did. The chroniclers disagree, and he was over 60.

claims.text: His great Shahnameh was broken up and sold page by page.
claims.note: The American collector Arthur Houghton split it up from the 1970s. In 1994 Iran swapped a de Kooning painting for the pages he still had.

claims.text: He banned wine and painting at his court in a fit of repentance.
claims.note: Tahmasp describes his repentance in his own memoir. How strictly the bans worked outside the palace is unclear.

reigns.hook: His son Ismail II kills most of his brothers and dies within a year, perhaps poisoned. The next shah is half blind and losing land on every side.

reigns.tagline: He built half the world and blinded his own sons
reigns.cameToPower: Put on the throne by a coup
reigns.previously: Half-blind Mohammad Khodabanda is losing land on every side.
paragraphs: Abbas was 17 when Qizilbash chiefs pushed his father aside and made him shah. He trusted none of them. First he bought time, giving the Ottomans a big slice of land in 1590 so he could deal with the Uzbeks. Then he built his own army of ghulams, slave soldiers drawn from Georgian, Armenian and Circassian converts, loyal only to him, plus musketeers and cannon.

In 1598 he made Isfahan his capital and rebuilt it around a vast square, Naqsh-e Jahan, lined with the Shah Mosque and the Ali Qapu palace. In 1605 he moved Armenian merchants from Julfa into a new suburb, New Julfa, to run his silk trade. He won back Tabriz, took Hormuz from the Portuguese with the help of English ships in 1622 and seized Baghdad in 1623.

He was also terrifyingly cruel. His campaigns in Georgia killed and deported people in huge numbers. Fearing plots, he had his eldest son Mohammad Baqer killed in 1615 and other sons blinded. When he died in 1629 there was no grown son left fit to rule. The throne went to his grandson Safi.

claims.text: The English brothers Anthony and Robert Shirley modernised his army.
claims.note: The Shirleys and their friends said so. Historians think Abbas's reforms were already under way and the brothers' role was small.

claims.text: The saying 'Isfahan is half the world' comes from his time.
claims.note: It rhymes in Persian and is usually linked to his new capital, but no one knows who first said it.

claims.text: Abbas walked the bazaars in disguise to see how his people lived.
claims.note: A favourite folk tale, told about many Persian rulers.

reigns.hook: Safi is a teenager who grew up behind harem walls. From now on Safavid princes are raised locked away, far from armies and provinces.

reigns.title: Princes from the Harem
reigns.tagline: Three shahs raised in the harem, and an empire coasting
reigns.previously: Shah Abbas dies, and the throne goes to his grandson Safi.
paragraphs: Abbas had made sure no son could plot against him, and his heirs paid for it. Princes now grew up shut away in the harem among women and eunuchs, with no experience of armies or provinces. Safi, still a teenager, took the throne in 1629 and soon purged courtiers and relatives. In 1639 the Treaty of Zuhab gave Baghdad to the Ottomans for good and drew a border close to today's line between Iran and Iraq.

His son Abbas II came to the throne as a boy in 1642 and turned out sharp and capable, though fond of drink. He took Kandahar back from the Mughals in 1649 and built the Chehel Sotoun in Isfahan, a palace hall with painted walls and a tall wooden porch reflected in a long pool. The name means forty columns. The porch has twenty.

His son was crowned as Safi II in 1666. Illness and bad omens followed, so the astrologers advised a fresh start, and he was crowned again as Suleiman. He left the business of government to the harem and his officials. The French jeweller Jean Chardin, who sold gems at his court, wrote down its luxury in loving detail. Suleiman died in 1694.

claims.text: Raising princes in the harem ruined the dynasty.
claims.note: European visitors and later historians loved this explanation. Some historians now think the system kept the peace and the real decline came later.

claims.text: Suleiman was crowned twice, under two different names.
claims.note: Persian court chroniclers and Chardin both describe the second coronation.

claims.text: Drink helped kill Abbas II in his thirties.
claims.note: Visitors and chroniclers mention his drinking. Others put his death down to disease.

reigns.hook: The new shah, Soltan Hoseyn, is gentle, pious and agrees with whoever spoke last. Far to the east, in Kandahar, the Afghan tribes are growing restless.

reigns.tagline: The gentle shah who lost Isfahan to hunger and Afghans
reigns.previously: Suleiman dies after a reign spent mostly in the harem.
paragraphs: Soltan Hoseyn was kind, devout and easy to talk round. The powerful cleric Mohammad-Baqer Majlesi had his ear, and pressure grew on Sunnis, Sufis and non-Muslims. That mattered, because the empire's eastern frontier was full of Sunni Afghans with grievances. Meanwhile the army was underpaid and the treasury was running dry.

In 1709 Mir Wais Hotak, a chief of the Ghilzai Afghans, killed the Persian governor of Kandahar and took the city. In 1722 his son Mahmud marched across the desert with a small army and on 8 March routed a much bigger Safavid force at Gulnabad, just outside Isfahan. Then he surrounded the capital.

The siege dragged on from March to October. Food ran out, and people ate leather, bark and worse. Huge numbers starved. In October 1722 Soltan Hoseyn rode out and surrendered. He lived on as a prisoner until the Afghans killed him a few years later. But one of his sons, Tahmasp, had slipped out of the city before the end, and he claimed the throne.

claims.text: Courtiers nicknamed him 'Very Well' because he agreed to everything.
claims.note: Said to come from his stock answer to any request. It appears in later writers and suits his reputation a bit too neatly.

claims.text: Soltan Hoseyn placed the crown on Mahmud's head with his own hands.
claims.note: Told by the Polish Jesuit Krusinski, who was in Isfahan, and by later chroniclers. The details differ between accounts.

claims.text: Tens of thousands died in the siege of Isfahan.
claims.note: Eyewitnesses describe mass starvation, but estimates of the dead vary widely and none is reliable.

reigns.hook: Afghans rule Isfahan. Russia and the Ottomans grab the north and west. Tahmasp II has a title but no army, until a tough Khorasan warlord offers his sword.

reigns.tagline: The nobody who looted Delhi and was killed in his tent
reigns.previously: Isfahan falls to the Afghans, and Prince Tahmasp escapes north.
paragraphs: Nader came from the Afshar, a Turkmen tribe in Khorasan, and from nowhere special. He rose as a soldier and warband leader, and in 1726 joined the exiled Tahmasp II, who named him Tahmasp Qoli Khan, 'slave of Tahmasp'. In 1729 he beat the Afghans at Mihmandust and again near Isfahan, and gave the capital back to his master. Then he drove back the Ottomans and got the Russians to hand back the Caspian provinces.

In 1732 he deposed Tahmasp and put the shah's baby son on the throne as Abbas III. On 8 March 1736, at a great assembly on the Mughan plain, Nader had himself proclaimed shah. He even tried to bring Shi'a and Sunni Islam closer together. In 1739 he invaded Mughal India, beat its army at Karnal and entered Delhi. When a riot broke out he ordered a massacre, and tens of thousands were killed in a day.

He came home with the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor diamond. But he grew suspicious and cruel. In 1742 he had his eldest son Reza Qoli blinded, believing he had plotted to kill him. Taxes soared and revolts were crushed savagely. In June 1747, in his camp at Quchan, his own officers broke into his tent and killed him.

claims.text: About 20,000 to 30,000 people were killed in the Delhi massacre.
claims.note: That is the range most historians give. Figures from the time vary much more widely.

claims.text: Nader named the diamond himself, crying 'Koh-i-Noor!', 'Mountain of Light!', when he first saw it.
claims.note: The story comes from later writers. The name certainly dates from his time or soon after.

claims.text: He had his eldest son Reza Qoli blinded.
claims.note: Recorded by his own court historian and by Europeans in Iran. Nader is said to have regretted it bitterly.

reigns.hook: Nader's empire shatters overnight. His heirs turn on each other, and in the Zagros mountains a Zand chief named Karim starts gathering men.

reigns.tagline: The chief who ruled Iran and never called himself shah
reigns.relationToPredecessor: No relation; a Zand tribal chief
reigns.cameToPower: Won the wars after Nader's death
reigns.previously: Nader Shah is murdered in his tent, and his empire falls apart.
paragraphs: Nader Shah's empire did not outlive him. His heirs turned on each other, and his blind grandson Shahrokh was left holding Mashhad in the far east. The rest of Iran became a brawl of warlords. Out of the Zagros mountains came Karim, chief of the Zand, a small Lak tribe. By about 1751 he was the strongest of them, and over the next ten years he beat his rivals one by one.

Karim never took the title of shah. He ruled as Vakil, the deputy, at first in the name of a Safavid boy, Ismail III, whom he kept as a puppet. He made Shiraz his capital and gave it buildings that still stand: the Vakil Bazaar, the Vakil Mosque and the Vakil Bath. Taxes were light and the roads were safe, and Iranians still remember him as the gentlest ruler of a brutal century.

In 1776 his army took Basra from the Ottomans. At his court lived an honoured hostage, the Qajar prince Agha Mohammad, whose tribe were the Zands' great rivals. Karim died in Shiraz on 1 March 1779, in his seventies, and left no son strong enough to hold what he had built.

claims.text: He called himself Vakil al-Ra'aya, 'deputy of the people'.
claims.note: He certainly ruled as Vakil. Historians differ on when he used the fuller title and how official it was.

claims.text: Karim Khan was the most humane ruler of 18th-century Iran.
claims.note: Persian chroniclers and European visitors praised his justice and low taxes. He could still be harsh with rebels, and he looked kind partly because the times were so cruel.

claims.text: A robbed merchant told Karim he had slept soundly because he thought the Vakil was awake, and Karim paid for his loss.
claims.note: A favourite anecdote in later Persian tellings. No record from his own time backs it up.

reigns.hook: Karim Khan is dead, and the Zand princes are already fighting over Shiraz. That same day the Qajar hostage Agha Mohammad slips out of the city and rides north to raise his tribe.

reigns.tagline: The eunuch who forged a dynasty in blood
reigns.cameToPower: Fought the Zands for the throne
reigns.reignEnded: Murdered in his tent at Shusha
reigns.previously: Karim Khan is dead, and his hostage Agha Mohammad has escaped.
paragraphs: Agha Mohammad was the son of a chief of the Qajars, a Turkic tribe from Astarabad near the Caspian. As a boy he was castrated on the orders of Nader Shah's nephew Adel Shah, so that he could never rule. He grew up beardless and high-voiced, and nobody who crossed him forgot it. He then spent years as a hostage at Karim Khan's court in Shiraz, treated well and quietly furious.

When Karim died in 1779 he escaped and gathered the Qajars. In 1786 he made Tehran, then a modest town, his capital. The young Zand prince Lotf Ali Khan fought him for years. In 1794 Agha Mohammad took Kerman, where Lotf Ali had held out, and punished it terribly: thousands of its men were blinded or killed. Lotf Ali was captured, blinded and put to death.

In 1795 he sacked Tbilisi to drag Georgia back from Russia's orbit, and in 1796 he was at last crowned shah. He had Nader's blind grandson Shahrokh tortured to give up the last of Nader's jewels. In June 1797, camped at Shusha in the Caucasus, he condemned two servants to death but put off the execution till morning. That night they killed him in his tent.

claims.text: As a hostage he secretly slashed Karim Khan's carpets with a knife.
claims.note: Told in later Qajar-era and European accounts. It fits his reputation but cannot be checked.

claims.text: The eyes of Kerman's men were brought to him and counted, 20,000 in some accounts.
claims.note: Mass blindings at Kerman are widely reported. The exact number comes from later accounts and may be inflated.

claims.text: He was castrated as a boy on Adel Shah's orders.
claims.note: Reported by Persian chroniclers and accepted by modern historians.

reigns.hook: His killers run off with the crown jewels, but the dynasty holds. Agha Mohammad had already picked his heir: his nephew Baba Khan, governor in Shiraz, who hurries north to take the throne.
